options: Supervised learning needs training examples that already carry the answer
Regression predicts a continuous numeric value
Clustering needs a labelled target column
A classification model outputs a category rather than a number
answer: Supervised learning needs training examples that already carry the answer
Regression predicts a continuous numeric value
A classification model outputs a category rather than a number
questions.explain: Supervised learning learns from labelled examples, and splits into regression, which predicts a number, and classification, which predicts a category. Clustering is unsupervised: it groups similar records without any labels, which is exactly why teams reach for it when nothing is labelled yet.
questions.teach: Machine learning finds patterns in data instead of following hand-written rules. In supervised learning, every training example comes with the right answer, called a label, and the model learns to predict that label for new data. The label can be a number, such as a house price, or a category, such as spam or not spam. In unsupervised learning there are no labels at all, so the model looks for structure on its own, for example by grouping similar records together.
hints: Three of the four statements are true and one is false, so your job is to find the odd one out. Focus on what the data must contain and what the model gives back, then ask whether each statement matches how that kind of learning really works.

The word label is the key. For each statement, ask whether the approach it describes uses a column that already holds the right answer. Then check the output types: a number that can take any value in a range is one kind of task, while a fixed set of named groups is another.

One statement gives an approach a requirement that the approach does not have. Picture a pile of customer records where nobody has tagged anything yet, and you still want similar customers grouped together. Could that job demand a target column? Whichever option contradicts this is the one to leave out.
questions.deep: Regression and classification both need labels, which is why both are supervised. Clustering, such as k-means, optimises a similarity measure with no target, so you judge it by inspection or a silhouette score rather than accuracy. A classifier that outputs a probability is still classification, because the final decision is a category.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the AI capability that satisfies it.
rows: Turn a recorded meeting into a written transcript
Convert a Norwegian support ticket into English for a London team
Decide whether a product review reads as positive or negative
Find and box every product logo in a shelf photo
answer: Speech to text
Translation
Sentiment analysis
Object detection
questions.explain: Speech to text and text to speech are opposite directions of the same pairing, and mixing them up is a common exam trap. Translation changes language while preserving meaning; sentiment analysis judges tone; object detection locates things in an image.
questions.teach: AI services are often named by the job they do on an input. Speech services work with spoken audio, either listening to it or producing it. Language services work with written text, for example changing it into another language or judging its mood. Vision services work with pictures, for example describing a photo or finding things inside it, and generative image models create new pictures from a written prompt. A good habit is to name the input and the output of any task first.
hints: Each requirement starts with a type of input and ends with a type of output or judgement. Before looking at the options, write down for each row what goes in (audio, text or an image) and what comes out. The matching capability is the one that does exactly that conversion or analysis.

Two options involve spoken audio but run in opposite directions, so check which side the audio is on for the row. Another option changes the language of text while keeping its meaning, and another judges how the writer feels. One more finds where things are in a picture, and the last creates new pictures from a prompt.

Three of the rows are about understanding something that already exists: a recording, a ticket in another language, a review's mood. The fourth is about locating items within an image. Two options are not needed here: one produces audio from written words, and one creates new images rather than analysing existing ones.
questions.deep: The Azure speech service covers both directions of audio and text, a translator service changes language, a language service scores sentiment, and a vision service detects objects. Detection returns bounding boxes with labels and confidence, while classification gives one label for the whole image, a split the exam likes to test.

questions.prompt: A warehouse app must analyse a photo and draw a box around each forklift and pallet, with a label for each one. Which computer vision capability should you use?
answer: Object detection
questions.explain: Object detection returns each object it finds together with its location, usually as a bounding box plus a label. Image classification labels the picture as a whole and returns no coordinates, OCR reads text, and face detection only locates faces.
questions.teach: Computer vision capabilities differ in what they return about a picture. Some return a single label for the whole image, such as warehouse. Some read text printed in the image. Some find only faces. Some create new images from a description. Others find individual things in the picture and report where each one sits, usually as a rectangle given by coordinates, with a label for each. Location is the detail that separates these output shapes.
hints: Read the requirement carefully: a box around each forklift and each pallet, with a label on every box. The answer must return several items per photo, each with a position, not one answer for the whole picture.

Ask which options return coordinates. A label for the whole image has no position. Reading text returns characters. Creating an image goes the wrong direction entirely, since the photo already exists.

Face detection does return locations, but only for faces, and forklifts have none. Image classification labels the whole picture once. Keep the option that finds many kinds of objects and returns a box and a label for each.
questions.deep: Object detection returns a bounding box plus a label for each object it finds. The exam contrast is with image classification, which labels the whole image and returns no coordinates. Whenever a scenario says draw a box or locate items, think object detection.

questions.prompt: An accounts team scans paper invoices and needs the printed and handwritten text pulled out as machine-readable characters. Which capability does this?
answer: Optical character recognition
questions.explain: Optical character recognition reads text out of images and scanned documents, including handwriting. Image classification and object detection describe what is in the picture rather than reading it, and sentiment analysis works on text you already have.
questions.teach: Scanned invoices are pictures to a computer: a grid of coloured dots, not letters. Before any program can search or process the words, something must recognise the shapes of printed and handwritten letters and turn them into characters. Other vision capabilities describe what is in a picture, such as objects or a label for the whole scene, and text analysis capabilities work on text that is already characters.
hints: Start with the input. A scanned invoice is an image, so the text on it is not yet text a computer can read. The capability you need turns shapes in an image into letters and numbers.

Ask which options read rather than describe. Labelling a picture or boxing objects tells you what is in the image, such as an invoice or a logo, but it does not give you the words and figures printed on it.

Sentiment analysis needs text that already exists, so it would have nothing to work on here. Image classification and object detection describe the picture. Only one option reads printed and handwritten characters.
questions.deep: OCR gives characters, not meaning: it cannot tell which number is the invoice total. When a question needs named fields such as total or due date, the answer moves up to Document Intelligence or a Content Understanding analyzer with a field schema.

questions.prompt: Users upload a photo of an existing product and ask the app to describe what is visible in it. Which capability should the app use?
options: A vision-enabled chat model that receives the image in the prompt
answer: A vision-enabled chat model that receives the image in the prompt
questions.explain: Interpreting an image that already exists is a job for a multimodal model that accepts image input and answers in text. An image-generation model works the other way round: it takes text and produces a new picture. The two speech options do not handle images at all.
questions.teach: Some models only read and write text. Multimodal models can also take other kinds of input, such as images, and answer in text. Image-generation models work in the opposite direction: they take a text description and create a picture. Speech features deal with audio, turning speech into text or text into speech. The direction of travel, from image to words or from words to image, is what separates these.
hints: Ask which direction the data flows. The user already has a photo and wants words back about what is in it. Something that makes a new picture would be running in the wrong direction.
The input is an image, so any option that only handles sound can go. Both speech-related options take or produce audio, and neither of them can look at a picture.
Image generation takes text and returns a new image, which is the reverse of this task. The remaining option is a model that accepts the photo as part of its input and replies with a description.
questions.deep: Vision-enabled chat models accept images inside the user message and answer in text. The exam trap is image generation: generation creates, vision interprets. Ask whether the picture exists before the call or after it.

questions.prompt: A marketing team needs an original image of a rural scene for its website, created from a written description. What should the team do in Microsoft Foundry?
options: Deploy a text-only chat model and ask it to draw the scene
Deploy an image-generation model and give it the description as a prompt
Run optical character recognition over existing stock photos
Use a vision model to describe a photo from a web search
answer: Deploy an image-generation model and give it the description as a prompt
questions.explain: Creating a new picture from text is image generation, and Foundry offers image-generation models you deploy and prompt like any other model. A text-only model can only return text, OCR reads text out of images, and describing someone else's photo does not create an original one.
questions.teach: Models in Foundry are specialised by output. A chat model returns text. A vision-enabled model reads images and returns text about them. An image-generation model returns new pictures from a text prompt. Separately, optical character recognition reads letters out of existing images. To pick one, ask what the team will hold at the end: words, or a picture that did not exist before.
hints: The team wants an original picture made from written words. Ask which options would end with a new image, and which would end with text about an image that already exists somewhere.

A text-only chat model can describe a scene in words, but it has no way to return a picture. Reading text out of stock photos and describing a web photo both start from someone else's image, which is not original.
Of the four, only one option deploys a model whose output is an image and feeds it the written description. The others either return text or work on photos that already exist.
questions.deep: Image-generation models are deployed and prompted like any other Foundry model, and content filters apply to them too. The exam pairs this with the reverse task, describing a photo, which needs a vision-enabled chat model instead.

questions.prompt: An app sends one request to a vision-enabled model deployment: a question plus an image URL. The response must come back as fast as possible. How should the request be structured?
options: One user message with the text, and the image sent in a second request
A system message with the text, and the image sent in a second request
One system message whose content array holds both the text and the image
One user message whose content array holds both a text item and an image item
answer: One user message whose content array holds both a text item and an image item
questions.explain: A user message's content can be an array that mixes a text part and an image part, so one round trip carries both. Splitting them doubles the calls and the model sees them as separate turns. The system message holds instructions, not the user's material.
questions.teach: A chat request is a list of messages, each with a role. The system message holds instructions for the assistant: its role and its rules. User messages hold what the person is asking about. With vision-enabled models, a message's content does not have to be one plain string; it can be a list of parts, where each part is either text or an image. Every separate request is another network round trip, which adds delay.
hints: The requirement is speed, so count the round trips each option needs. Any option that sends the image in a second request doubles the calls and adds waiting time before the answer arrives.
Next, ask which role owns the material. The question and the image come from the user. The system message is for the assistant's instructions, not for the user's content.

Two options split the request in two, so they fail the speed test. Of the two single-request options, one puts the user's material in the instructions slot. Pick the one that keeps it in the user's own message.
questions.deep: Mixing a text part and an image part in one user message is the standard multimodal request shape. Splitting them costs a second call and the model sees two separate turns. The exam also tests the trap of putting user material in the system message.

questions.prompt: A Python app sends a local JPEG to a vision-enabled chat model as binary data. What should the image_url url field contain?
answer: data:image/jpeg;base64,<encoded bytes>
questions.explain: The model service cannot read your disk, so a local file travels inside the request as a base64 data URL. A Windows path, a file:// URL or a bare filename all point at a place only your own machine can open.
questions.teach: When an app calls a cloud model, the model runs on a server far away that cannot see your computer's files. Anything the model needs has to travel inside the request itself. Binary data such as an image can be converted into plain text with an encoding called base64, and wrapped in a data URL, a web address format that carries the content itself rather than a location where the content lives.
hints: Think about where the model runs. It is on a remote service, not on your laptop, so any answer that points at a place on your own disk only works for your own machine.
Three of the options are ways of naming a location on the local machine: a Windows path, a file URL and a bare file name. Ask what the service would do with an address it has no access to.
The remaining option does not point anywhere. It carries the image bytes, encoded as text, inside the request itself, which is what a remote service needs when the image lives only on your machine.
questions.deep: A local path is the classic mistake: it looks right in code and fails because the service cannot open it. The prefix names the media type, so a PNG needs image/png rather than image/jpeg, and the bytes after the comma are the base64 text.

questions.prompt: A company holds thousands of recorded support calls as audio files in Azure Storage and needs a written transcript of each one. Which Azure Speech capability fits?
answer: Batch transcription
questions.explain: Batch transcription is built for large amounts of stored audio: you point it at the files or a storage container, it transcribes them concurrently, and you collect the results asynchronously. Real-time speech to text is for live audio as it is spoken, text to speech runs the other way, and translation changes language.
questions.teach: Azure Speech offers several capabilities that differ in direction and timing. Some turn spoken audio into text, some turn text into spoken audio, and some change the language. Timing matters too: live audio is handled as it is spoken, with instant results, while large collections of stored recordings can be processed as a background job, many files at once, with results collected later.
hints: The recordings already exist, sitting in storage, and there are thousands of them. Nobody is speaking live. Ask which option is designed for a large pile of stored audio rather than a live conversation.

The output is a written transcript, so the direction is audio to text. That rules out the option that turns text into audio, and the option that changes language, because nobody asked for another language.

Real-time speech to text also goes from audio to text, but it is built for audio as it is being spoken. For thousands of stored files processed together and collected later, pick the option built for bulk jobs.
questions.deep: Batch transcription points at files or a storage container, transcribes them concurrently and returns results asynchronously. The exam contrast is live versus stored: real-time for a call in progress, batch for archives.

questions.prompt: A utility company wants written outage notices turned into natural-sounding speech that its phone system can play to callers. Which Speech capability should it use?
answer: Speech synthesis
questions.explain: Speech synthesis, also called text to speech, turns text into spoken audio in a chosen neural voice. Speech recognition goes from audio to text, speaker recognition identifies who is talking, and translation converts between languages.
questions.teach: Speech features go in two directions. Recognition features listen to audio and produce text, or identify who is speaking. Other features take text and produce audio in a natural-sounding voice chosen from a set of neural voices. A third kind changes the language of speech. The phrase text to speech names one direction and speech to text names the other, and many exam questions are built on mixing them up.
hints: Check the direction. The input is written outage notices and the output is audio that a phone system plays. Anything that starts from audio and produces text is running the wrong way.
Speech recognition and speaker recognition both start from audio: one writes down the words, the other identifies the person talking. Neither can take written notices and read them aloud.
Speech translation changes language, and nobody asked for a new language. The remaining option produces spoken audio from text, which is the job the phone system needs done.
questions.deep: Speech synthesis is the formal name for text to speech, and the voice is chosen by name in the speech configuration. The exam lists synonyms side by side, so learn both names: recognition is speech to text, synthesis is text to speech.

questions.prompt: In a Python app built with the Azure Speech SDK, which class holds the key and endpoint used to connect to the Speech service?
answer: speechsdk.SpeechConfig
questions.explain: SpeechConfig carries the connection details, the key and endpoint, plus settings such as the voice name. The audio config classes say where sound comes from or goes to, and SpeechSynthesizer is the object that does the work once it has been handed both configs.
questions.teach: SDKs usually split setup into separate objects with separate jobs. One object holds connection details: which service to reach and how to prove you may use it, plus service-wide settings. Other objects describe where audio comes from or where it goes, such as a microphone, a speaker or a file. A worker object then takes those setup objects and does the actual recognition or synthesis.
hints: The question asks about connection details: the key and the endpoint. Ask which class sounds like it describes the service connection, rather than a microphone, a speaker or the worker that produces speech.
Two options live in the audio namespace. Audio configuration classes describe where sound comes from or goes to, so they answer a different question than how to reach the service.

The synthesizer is the worker that does the job once it has been handed its configuration objects, so it uses the connection details rather than holding them. One remaining class is the service configuration.
questions.deep: SpeechConfig carries the key, the endpoint and settings such as the voice name; the audio config classes say where sound comes from or goes; the synthesizer takes both and does the work. Recognise the config-then-worker shape and these SDK questions get easy.

questions.prompt: A voice support app takes a spoken question and answers out loud using a deployed model. Arrange the steps from first to last.
tray: Convert the model's reply to speech
Capture the customer's spoken question
Play the audio back to the customer
Send the text to the deployed model
Convert the speech to text
answer: Capture the customer's spoken question
Convert the speech to text
Send the text to the deployed model
Convert the model's reply to speech
Play the audio back to the customer
questions.explain: Speech to text feeds the model, and text to speech carries the answer back, so the pipeline runs audio, text, model, text, audio. OCR reads text in images and has no role with sound. The skills outline also covers a deployed multimodal model answering a spoken prompt directly, which merges the first three steps into one call.
questions.teach: A voice assistant chains several capabilities together, and each one changes the form of the data. Speech recognition turns sound into words. A language model reads words and writes words. Speech synthesis turns words back into sound. Because each step can only accept the form the previous step produced, the order is forced by the data types, not by preference.
hints: Follow the form of the data. It starts as sound from the customer and has to end as sound played back to them. Work out where it must be text in between, since the model reads and writes text.
The model can only read text, so the spoken question has to be turned into text before it is sent. The model's reply is text too, so it needs converting back to audio before anything can be played.

Pair the conversions with their neighbours: capture sits before speech to text, the model sits between the two conversions, and playback is the very last step. If audio ever reaches the model directly, a step is out of order.
questions.deep: The pipeline runs audio, text, model, text, audio. The web drill adds an OCR distractor, which reads text in images and has no role with sound. The skills outline also covers a multimodal model answering a spoken prompt directly, which merges the first three steps into one call.

questions.prompt: An app uses the Responses API to send a prompt to a vision-enabled model deployed in Foundry, and must include an image for the model to analyse. Which content item type carries the image?
answer: input_image
questions.explain: In the Responses API, content you send is typed input_text or input_image, so an image for analysis goes in an input_image item, either as a URL or as a base64 data URL. output_image and image_generation relate to producing images, and image_base64 is not an item type.
questions.teach: Requests to a multimodal model are built from typed content items. Each item says what it is and which direction it travels. In the Responses API, anything you send starts with input_, such as input_text for words and input_image for pictures. Items the model sends back are output items.
hints: Ask which direction the image travels. You are sending it to the model for analysis, so the item type should describe something going in, not something coming out.
Two options are about making images, which is the opposite of analysing one. Set those aside, because the model here only looks at a picture you supply.
Base64 is one way to encode the image data inside the item, not the name of the item type. The item type follows the same naming pattern as input_text.
questions.deep: The image itself sits in image_url, either as an https URL or as data:image/jpeg;base64,... for local bytes. The older Chat Completions API uses a user message whose content array has text and image_url items. Both shapes appear in AI-901 labs.

questions.prompt: Which of these tasks can Azure AI Vision perform?
options: Extract key phrases from a set of documents
Extract the text from scanned handwritten letters
Identify animal breeds in live video streams
answer: Extract the text from scanned handwritten letters
questions.explain: Azure AI Vision's OCR (Read) feature extracts printed and handwritten text from images. Key phrase extraction is a Language feature, and video thumbnails and live breed identification are not Vision image analysis features.
questions.teach: Azure AI Vision analyses still images. Its main features are captions, tags, object detection, people detection, smart cropping, and OCR, which reads printed and handwritten text. Tasks on plain text belong to Azure Language, and custom categories such as specific breeds need a custom-trained model.
hints: Ask whether each task works on an image, on text, or on video. Azure AI Vision's home ground is a still image, including a scanned page.
Key phrase extraction runs on text that is already machine-readable, so it belongs to the Language service, not to a vision service.
The two video options need either video processing or a custom-trained model. Reading handwriting from a scanned page is the built-in OCR capability.
questions.deep: OCR in Azure AI Vision handles both printed and handwritten text across many languages. For structured fields from forms, such as invoice totals, the exam prefers Document Intelligence or Content Understanding over plain OCR.

questions.prompt: For which two workloads can you use computer vision? Choose two.
options: Describing the contents of an image in a sentence
Assigning each pixel in an image to the object it belongs to
Detecting anomalies in a stream of sensor data
Creating charts that visualise numerical data
answer: Describing the contents of an image in a sentence
Assigning each pixel in an image to the object it belongs to
questions.explain: Labelling each pixel is image segmentation and writing a sentence about an image is captioning; both are computer vision because both analyse images. Sensor anomaly detection works on numbers over time, and charting is data visualisation.
questions.teach: Computer vision means software that interprets images or video. Its common tasks are classification (what is this image of?), object detection (where are the things?), segmentation (which pixels belong to which thing?), OCR (what text is shown?) and captioning (describe the scene). Producing a picture from data is visualisation, not vision.
hints: Ask whether each workload takes an image as its input. Computer vision interprets pictures; it does not create charts or read sensor streams.
Anomaly detection on sensor data works on numbers over time. There is no picture anywhere in that task, so it is not a vision workload.
Charts are pictures made from numbers, which is the opposite direction. The two remaining workloads both read an image: one labels pixels, the other describes the scene.
questions.deep: Segmentation assigns every pixel to an object, while object detection draws a bounding box. Exam scenarios about precise outlines, such as weeds between crop rows, point to segmentation, and 'where is each item' points to detection.

questions.prompt: A quality team plans to use object detection on photos from a production line. Which three can object detection do? Choose three.
options: Find the location of a damaged product in an image
Read the serial number printed on each product
Find several damaged products in the same image
Tell apart several different types of damaged product in one image
answer: Find the location of a damaged product in an image
Find several damaged products in the same image
Tell apart several different types of damaged product in one image
questions.explain: Object detection returns a bounding box and a label for each object it finds, so it locates objects, finds several instances, and distinguishes several classes in one image. Reading a printed serial number is OCR.
questions.teach: Object detection answers where the things are and what each thing is. For every object it finds, it returns a label and a bounding box. It handles many objects and many types in one picture. It does not read text; turning pixels of letters into characters is a separate capability called OCR.
hints: Recall what object detection returns for each object it finds: a label and a box around it. Check each option against that output.
A box plus a label can be repeated for every object in a picture, and the labels can differ. So think about whether several items, or several kinds of item, cause a problem.
Reading a serial number means turning the shapes of letters into characters. Object detection could find where the label is, but reading it is a different capability.
questions.deep: Custom detection of domain objects, such as specific defect types, needs a model trained on your own labelled images. Older exams name Custom Vision for this. Know the principle: prebuilt models know common objects, and custom classes need training.

questions.prompt: Which Azure AI Vision feature generates a human-readable sentence describing a photograph?
answer: Image captioning
questions.explain: Captioning, also called image description, writes a full sentence about the scene. Tagging returns single-word labels, categorization puts the image into a broad category, and type detection says whether it is a photo or clip art.
questions.teach: Image analysis can return several kinds of description. Tags are single words such as dog, beach or sky. Categories are broad buckets such as outdoor or food. A caption is a full sentence such as 'a dog running on a beach', written for a human to read. Only the caption is a sentence.
hints: The key words are human-readable sentence. Ask which feature outputs a full sentence rather than single words or a category name.
Tagging returns a list of labels such as dog and beach. That is useful for search, but it is a list of words, not a sentence.
Categorization and type detection each return one broad label about the whole image. Only one feature writes a description in natural language.
questions.deep: Azure AI Vision 4.0 offers captions and dense captions, which caption individual regions. For open-ended questions about an image, AI-901 also expects you to know that a vision-enabled chat model can describe images in whatever detail the prompt asks for.

questions.prompt: In which two scenarios would you use speech synthesis? Choose two.
options: A phone system reads back a card number the caller typed on the keypad
A character in a computer game speaks its lines aloud to the player
Live captions are generated for a news broadcast
Key phrases are extracted from a recorded meeting
answer: A phone system reads back a card number the caller typed on the keypad
A character in a computer game speaks its lines aloud to the player
questions.explain: Speech synthesis turns text into spoken audio, which is what the phone read-back and the game character need. Live captions need speech to text, and key phrases from a recording need speech to text followed by text analysis.
questions.teach: Speech has two directions. Speech recognition, or speech to text, listens to audio and writes down the words. Speech synthesis, or text to speech, takes text and speaks it aloud in a natural voice. Most speech questions come down to which direction the data flows.
hints: For each scenario, ask what the input is and what the output is. Synthesis must start with text and end with audio a person hears.
Captions start with someone speaking and end with written words, which is the opposite direction. Set that scenario aside.
Pulling key phrases from a meeting recording starts with audio too, so it needs transcription first. The two remaining scenarios both end with a voice speaking.
questions.deep: Azure Speech's neural voices produce synthesis, and SSML controls pronunciation, pauses and speaking style. For AI-901 labs, SpeechSynthesizer speaks text and SpeechRecognizer transcribes. Both take a SpeechConfig.

questions.prompt: While you present at a conference, your talk is turned into subtitles for the audience in real time. Which capability is this?
answer: Speech recognition
questions.explain: Turning spoken words into text as they are said is speech recognition, also called speech to text. Synthesis goes the other way, sentiment judges tone, and translation would only be needed if the subtitles were in another language.
questions.teach: Speech recognition listens to audio and produces text. In real time it powers live captions, and in batch mode it transcribes recordings. Speech synthesis is the reverse: text becomes audio. If the question adds 'in another language', translation joins in, and Azure offers speech translation for that case.
hints: Name the input and the output: the input is your voice, and the output is text on a screen. Ask which capability goes from audio to text.
Speech synthesis is the mirror image: it reads text aloud. Here nothing is being read aloud to the audience, so it cannot be the answer.
The scenario never says the subtitles are in a different language, so translation is not needed. Sentiment would only judge the tone of your words.
questions.deep: Real-time speech to text streams partial results as the speaker talks, and batch transcription processes stored files asynchronously. Choose batch for thousands of recordings in storage and real time for live captions.

questions.prompt: A voice app built with the Azure Speech SDK must listen for one short spoken command, turn it into text, and then stop listening. Which SpeechRecognizer method fits?
questions.code:
speech_config = speechsdk.SpeechConfig(subscription=key, region=region)
recognizer = speechsdk.SpeechRecognizer(speech_config=speech_config)
result = recognizer.____
answer: recognize_once()
questions.explain: recognize_once() listens for a single utterance, returns when the speaker pauses, and stops, which fits a one-off command. Continuous recognition keeps listening for long audio, keyword recognition waits for a wake word, and speak_text_async belongs to the synthesizer and speaks text aloud.
questions.teach: The Speech SDK's SpeechRecognizer has two main listening modes. Single-shot recognition captures one utterance and returns when the speaker stops talking, which suits short commands. Continuous recognition runs until you stop it and raises events as text arrives, which suits dictation, meetings and long files.
hints: The command is short and the app should stop after it. Ask which method's name says it captures a single piece of speech and then returns.
Continuous recognition keeps running until you stop it, which suits meetings or long recordings rather than one quick command.
Keyword recognition waits for a wake word, and the method that speaks text belongs to the synthesizer, not the recognizer. One method remains.
questions.deep: recognize_once() stops after the first utterance and caps how much audio it will take, so it is wrong for long files. For a long recording, use continuous recognition with the recognized event, or batch transcription for many stored files.

questions.prompt: An app uses the Speech SDK to turn text into speech and must save the audio to a WAV file instead of playing it. What should audio_config be set to before creating the SpeechSynthesizer?
answer: speechsdk.audio.AudioOutputConfig(filename="output.wav")
questions.explain: AudioOutputConfig says where synthesized audio goes, and its filename argument writes it to a file. The default-speaker version plays the audio aloud, AudioConfig with a microphone configures input for recognition, and SpeechConfig holds the key and region, not the output destination.
questions.teach: The Speech SDK separates three concerns. SpeechConfig says how to connect: key, region or endpoint, voice. An audio config says where sound comes from or goes to: a microphone, a speaker, or a file. The synthesizer or recognizer combines the two. For synthesis, the output side is AudioOutputConfig.
hints: The audio is coming out of the service, not going into it. Look for the class whose name says output, then check which argument points at a file.
SpeechConfig holds connection details such as the key and region. Ask whether where the audio is saved belongs with connection details or with audio routing.
Two options use the output class. One sends audio to the speakers, the other writes it to disk. The requirement says a file.
questions.deep: If you pass audio_config=None, the result's audio_data holds the bytes in memory, which suits web apps that stream audio back. Output format, such as MP3 or WAV sample rate, is set on SpeechConfig with set_speech_synthesis_output_format.

questions.prompt: What does the Voice Live API in Azure Speech in Foundry Tools provide?
options: A batch service that transcribes stored audio files overnight
A tool for cloning a specific person's voice from a sample
Speech recognition, generative AI reasoning and speech synthesis combined in one low-latency interface for voice agents
Speech-to-text only; you must add a model and text-to-speech yourself
answer: Speech recognition, generative AI reasoning and speech synthesis combined in one low-latency interface for voice agents
questions.explain: Voice Live joins listening, reasoning with a generative model and speaking into one managed real-time API, so you do not wire three services together. It is not transcription-only, not a batch service, and not a voice-cloning tool.
questions.teach: A voice agent needs three stages: turn the user's speech into text, decide what to say with a language model, and turn the reply into speech. You can chain three services yourself, but every hand-off adds delay and code. Voice Live runs all three stages behind one real-time connection built for natural conversation.
hints: Think about the three stages a spoken conversation with an AI needs: hearing, thinking and speaking. Ask how much of that the API is meant to cover.
Batch transcription processes stored files and is not live at all, while Voice Live, as the name says, is about live conversation.
Speech-to-text-only would leave you building the other two stages yourself, which is exactly the effort this API is meant to remove.
questions.deep: Voice Live also handles conversational details such as interruptions, noise suppression and end-of-turn detection. AI-901's skill 'respond to spoken prompts by using a deployed multimodal model' is the other route: audio-capable models take audio in and return audio directly.

questions.prompt: A developer is testing image prompts with a vision-enabled model in Foundry. Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: The Responses API can take an image either as a URL or as base64-encoded data
You must deploy a text-only model because image handling happens in your app code
In the Foundry playground you can attach a local image and type a question in the same message
Images can only be sent as base64 data, never as a URL
answer: The Responses API can take an image either as a URL or as base64-encoded data
In the Foundry playground you can attach a local image and type a question in the same message
questions.explain: The playground supports attaching an image alongside text for multimodal models, and the API accepts a public URL or a data URL with base64 bytes. The word only makes the third statement false, and a text-only model cannot read images, so the model itself must be multimodal.
questions.teach: A vision-enabled, or multimodal, model reads images and text together in one prompt. You can try it in the Foundry playground by attaching a picture, and in code you pass the image in the request either as a link the service can fetch or as the raw bytes encoded in base64. The model does the seeing; your app only sends the picture.
hints: Two statements describe ways to get an image to the model, one in the portal and one in code. Two others restrict what is possible. Test the restrictions first.
A public image already on the web can simply be linked, while a file on your laptop cannot be fetched by the service. So think about whether both ways of sending an image are needed.
Ask where image understanding actually happens. If a text-only model received an image, nothing in it could interpret the pixels.
questions.deep: Words like only, must, never and always often mark false statements in yes/no grids. Local files go in as data:image/jpeg;base64,... and hosted files as https URLs. The model deployment must support vision, as GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 do.

questions.prompt: A finance team scans supplier PDFs and needs each invoice number, total and due date returned as named fields, not as a wall of text. Which capability fits best?
options: Optical character recognition on its own
answer: Document Intelligence field extraction
questions.explain: Document Intelligence reads the document and returns structured key-value pairs and tables, so a total arrives labelled as a total. Plain OCR gives you the characters but leaves you to work out which number is the invoice total, and the other two options answer different questions entirely.
questions.teach: Reading a document and understanding it are different jobs. Character recognition turns a scan into raw text, but leaves you with a wall of words and numbers where a total looks the same as a phone number. Document processing services go further: they return named fields and tables, so each value arrives labelled with what it is. Other capabilities classify whole images or pull out key phrases, which are different outputs again.
hints: The team says it does not want a wall of text. It wants each invoice number, total and due date returned as a named field. Keep that output shape in mind while you look at the options.

Plain character reading gets every figure off the page but does not know which figure is the total. Ask which option returns values already paired with their meaning, so a total arrives labelled as a total.

Image classification labels the whole picture, for example as an invoice, and key phrase extraction returns important phrases with no field names. One option is built to return structured key-value pairs and tables.
questions.deep: The exam trap here is always OCR on its own, which gives characters without meaning. A Content Understanding analyzer with a field schema solves the same kind of problem and appears elsewhere in this level, including nested fields such as line items.

questions.prompt: You are using Azure Content Understanding to process voicemail recordings. You need a transcript plus structured fields such as the caller's request. Which kind of analyzer should you base it on?
answer: An audio analyzer
questions.explain: Content Understanding has a base analyzer for each modality: document, image, audio and video. Voicemail is audio, so an audio analyzer transcribes the speech and then fills the fields you defined. A video analyzer would expect frames as well as sound.
questions.teach: Azure Content Understanding turns unstructured files into structured results. You start from a base analyzer that matches the kind of file you are sending: one for documents, one for images, one for audio and one for video. You then add the fields you want pulled out. The base analyzer decides how the file is read, for example whether speech is transcribed or whether frames are examined.
hints: Ask what a voicemail actually is as a file. It is a recording of someone speaking, with no pages and no pictures. The analyzer type follows the kind of file, not the kind of result you want out.
A document analyzer expects pages such as PDFs, and an image analyzer expects pictures. Neither can listen to a recording, so both answer a different question from the one being asked.
A video analyzer handles sound too, but it expects frames as well as audio, and a voicemail has no frames. Pick the analyzer that is built for sound on its own.
questions.deep: Every custom analyzer inherits from one of the four base analyzers. The audio one transcribes the speech and then fills the fields you defined. The exam tests the rule directly: pick the analyzer by what the file is, not by what you want out of it.

questions.prompt: A web app must pull fields, including nested values such as invoice line items, out of supplier invoices according to a schema you define. What should you use?
options: An OCR-only pipeline that returns the raw text
An analyzer in Azure Content Understanding with a field schema
An Azure AI Search index over the invoices
answer: An analyzer in Azure Content Understanding with a field schema
questions.explain: A Content Understanding analyzer applies a field schema, including nested and list fields, and returns structured values with confidence scores and grounding. OCR alone gives characters with no idea which number is the total, transcription is for audio, and a search index finds documents rather than extracting fields from them.
questions.teach: Pulling data out of documents comes in levels. The lowest level reads characters, giving raw text. A higher level applies a schema: a definition of the fields you want, such as vendor, total or a list of line items, each with a type. Results then come back as structured values, often with a confidence score and a pointer to where each value was found. Search indexes are a different tool again: they find documents, they do not fill fields.
hints: Note the phrase according to a schema you define, and that some fields are nested, like line items inside an invoice. The answer has to accept your own field definitions, not just read the page.
Raw text from OCR contains every number on the page, but it does not know which one is the total or which lines are items. Transcription is for audio and has no place with supplier invoices.
A search index helps you find the right invoice among thousands, but it does not extract fields from it. Keep the option that applies your field definitions and returns structured values.
questions.deep: A Content Understanding analyzer supports nested and list fields and returns values with confidence scores and grounding back to the source. On the exam, according to a schema or nested fields points here, while find the document points to search.

questions.prompt: Using the Content Understanding Python SDK, you submit a PDF to an analyzer and need the extraction results. What is the call pattern?
options: client.analyze(...), which returns the fields in the same response
Submit the PDF and read the fields from the response headers
Run OCR yourself and map the fields in your own code
answer: client.begin_analyze(...), then poller.result()
questions.explain: Analysis is a long-running operation, so the SDK starts it with begin_analyze and hands back a poller; poller.result() waits for completion and returns the analysis. That begin_... then result() shape is common across Azure SDKs, which makes it worth recognizing on sight.
questions.teach: Some cloud operations finish in milliseconds and some take seconds or minutes, such as analysing a long PDF. For slow ones, Azure SDKs use a long-running operation pattern: a call starts the job and immediately hands back a poller object, a handle you can use to wait for the job and fetch the result once it is done. Recognising which operations are long-running tells you which call pattern to expect.
hints: Analysing a whole PDF takes time. Ask whether a single call that returns the fields straight away fits a job that may run for many seconds, or whether you would expect to start the job and come back for it.
Response headers carry metadata about a request, not the extracted content, so reading fields out of them is not how results arrive. Doing the OCR yourself skips the analyzer entirely.
Compare the two SDK calls. One pretends the work is instant. The other starts the job, gets a handle, and waits on that handle for the finished analysis. The second shape matches a long-running task.
questions.deep: The begin_ prefix followed by result() on the returned poller is shared across Azure Python SDKs, so recognising it on sight answers several exam questions at once. result() waits until the operation completes and returns the analysis.

questions.prompt: A training department wants each training video split into scenes, with a description of each scene. Which Content Understanding analyzer type handles this requirement?
answer: Video analyzer
questions.explain: The four base analyzers map one-to-one to the input modality, and every custom analyzer inherits from one of them. Picking the type is a matter of asking what the file is, not what you want out of it, and a training video is video.
questions.teach: Azure Content Understanding sorts its analyzers by the kind of file they read, called the modality. There is one base analyzer per modality, and every custom analyzer you build inherits from one of them. A still picture, a page of text, a sound recording and moving pictures with sound are four different modalities, and each is read in its own way.
hints: Start with the file, not the goal. The department has training videos, so ask which modality those files are. Scenes and descriptions are what you want out, but the analyzer type follows what goes in.

A scene is a stretch of moving pictures over time. A single image has no time dimension, and an audio recording has no pictures, so each of those analyzers covers only part of what a training video contains.
A document analyzer reads pages such as PDFs, which a training video does not have. That leaves the one analyzer built for files with both frames and sound over time.
questions.deep: Splitting into scenes with a description of each is a signature output of the video analyzer. The same drill question maps PDFs to document, voicemails to audio and product photos to image, and the exam expects you to answer from the file type alone.

questions.prompt: An app processes voicemail recordings with Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools. Which feature turns the audio into text?
answer: Transcription
questions.explain: Content Understanding's audio analyzers first transcribe speech to text and then extract fields from the transcript. Key phrase extraction works on text that already exists, OCR reads text in images, and Voice Live is a real-time voice conversation API.
questions.teach: Content Understanding extracts structured information from documents, images, audio and video. For audio it works in two stages: it transcribes the speech into text, then applies your field schema to that transcript. Every modality has a first step that turns raw content into something the model can reason over.
hints: Think about what must happen first before anything can be extracted from a voicemail. The spoken words need to become written words.
OCR also produces text, but from pixels in an image, not from sound. Match the capability to the kind of input, which here is audio.
Key phrases can only be pulled from text that already exists, and Voice Live is for live two-way voice conversations. The remaining option names the audio-to-text step.
questions.deep: Audio analyzers return a transcript with speaker and timing information plus your custom fields, for example caller name or requested action. The video analyzer adds scene segmentation and key frames on top of transcription.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants descriptions of what appears on each of its product photos, returned as structured fields. Which Content Understanding analyzer type should it use?
answer: Image analyzer
questions.explain: The four base analyzers map one-to-one to the input modality, and a product photo is an image. Documents, video and audio each have their own analyzer, and every custom analyzer inherits from one of the four.
questions.teach: Content Understanding has four base analyzer types: document, image, audio and video. You choose the type by asking what kind of file you have, not what you want out of it. You then add a field schema describing what to extract, and the service returns those fields as structured JSON.
hints: The rule for choosing an analyzer is to look at the file, not the goal. Ask what kind of file a product photo is.
A document analyzer is for pages such as PDFs, invoices and forms. A photo of a product is not a page of text, even if a label appears in it.
Video and audio analyzers need time-based media. A single still photo leaves only one analyzer type.
questions.deep: Extract information from images by using Content Understanding is a named AI-901 skill. Image analyzers can return generated fields such as a description or category, alongside fields extracted from what is visible.

questions.prompt: In which two scenarios would you use a document-extraction service such as Azure Document Intelligence or a Content Understanding document analyzer? Choose two.
options: Extract the invoice number from a supplier invoice
Identify the retailer from a photographed receipt
Translate a letter from French to English
Find images of a product in an online catalog
answer: Extract the invoice number from a supplier invoice
Identify the retailer from a photographed receipt
questions.explain: Receipts and invoices are documents with known fields such as merchant name, totals and invoice numbers, which document extraction returns as structured data. Translation belongs to Translator, and searching a catalog for images is visual search.
questions.teach: Document extraction goes beyond OCR. OCR returns all the text on a page, while document extraction returns named fields, such as MerchantName, InvoiceId and Total, together with their values. Prebuilt models cover common documents like receipts, invoices and ID cards, and custom schemas cover your own forms.
hints: Ask whether each scenario starts with a business document and wants specific named values out of it. That pattern is exactly what document extraction is for.
Translating a letter changes its language but pulls out no fields. That is a job for a translation service, even though the input is a document.
Finding product images is a search over pictures. The two remaining scenarios both read a receipt or an invoice and return one named value.
questions.deep: On AI-901, Content Understanding is the named Foundry tool for document, image, audio and video extraction, and Document Intelligence still appears in older-style items. Both beat plain OCR whenever the question asks for named or nested fields.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the Content Understanding analyzer type that handles it.
rows: Pull the invoice number and total from supplier PDFs
Transcribe voicemails and extract the caller's request
Split a training video into scenes with a description of each
Describe what appears on product photos
answer: Document analyzer
Audio analyzer
Video analyzer
Image analyzer
questions.explain: The four base analyzers map one-to-one to the input modality, and every custom analyzer inherits from one of them. Picking the type is a matter of asking what the file is, not what you want out of it.
questions.teach: Content Understanding is an Azure service that turns messy files into structured fields you can store in a database. You configure an analyzer, a reusable definition of what to extract, and the service runs it on each file you send. Analyzers are organised by the kind of file they accept, because each kind of media needs different processing, such as reading page layout versus listening to speech.
hints: For this kind of question, ignore what you want out of the file and look only at what the file is. Read each row and underline the noun for the input, such as a PDF, a voicemail, a video or a photo.

There are four options and four rows, and the options are named for the kind of media they accept. Each row names the media it works on, even if only by its everyday word, so a recording of a spoken message is one kind and a moving recording with pictures is another. Pair the obvious ones first.

If two rows seem close, separate moving pictures from still ones, and page-based files from photographs. Decide whether each file is something you read, hear, watch or look at, then pick the option named for that kind of media. The goal in the sentence does not change which option fits.
questions.deep: Custom analyzers inherit from a base one and add a field schema, so you name fields such as InvoiceNumber and the service fills them in. The modality choice comes first, the schema second. A video analyzer also transcribes the speech in the video, so you rarely need a separate audio step.

questions.prompt: Before committing to one model, a team wants to browse the available models, compare them and pick a candidate to deploy. Which part of Foundry is designed for this?
answer: The model catalog
questions.explain: The model catalog is where you discover, compare and select models to deploy. The quota page tells you what throughput you may use, content filters govern what the model is allowed to say, and logs describe what already happened.
questions.teach: Microsoft Foundry is the platform where you pick, deploy and manage AI models. It has different areas for different stages. Before deployment you need somewhere to browse available models and compare them. After deployment you deal with quotas that limit traffic, content filters that limit what the model may say, and logs that record what happened. Asking which stage the team is in narrows the choice.
hints: The team has not deployed anything yet. They want to browse, compare and choose. Any option that only makes sense after a model is already deployed answers a different question.
Quotas govern how much traffic a deployment may send and content filters govern what a deployment may say. Both are settings on something you already have running, not places to shop for a model.

Deployment logs describe what already happened in a running system, so they are useful later but not before a choice is made. The remaining option is the place designed for discovering and selecting models.
questions.deep: The model catalog is the discovery point, and its model leaderboard compares models on quality, safety, estimated cost and throughput. The exam separates choices made before deployment from controls that apply after it, such as quota, filters and monitoring.

questions.prompt: An application starts returning throttling errors at peak hours. Which deployment property most directly governs how much traffic the application may send?
options: The tokens-per-minute quota on the deployment
answer: The tokens-per-minute quota on the deployment
questions.explain: Throughput is capped per deployment and measured in tokens per minute alongside a request rate. Exceeding it produces throttling responses. Temperature, system message and few-shot examples change what comes back, not how much traffic you are allowed to send.
questions.teach: A deployed model runs on shared capacity, so the platform limits how much each deployment may use. The limit is counted in tokens over time, together with a request rate. When an app sends more than its allowance, the service answers with throttling errors instead of results. Settings that shape a single answer are a different kind of control from settings that cap overall traffic.
hints: Throttling means the service is saying slow down, you are sending too much. Look for the option that sets a ceiling on traffic, rather than one that changes the wording or style of answers.

Peak hours is the clue. The errors appear only when many requests arrive at once, so the cause is volume, not the content of any single request. Which option is measured over time rather than per answer?

Temperature changes randomness, and system message length and few-shot examples change the prompt. Each affects what comes back from one call. Only one option limits how much traffic the deployment accepts.
questions.deep: Throughput is capped per deployment in tokens per minute alongside a request rate, and going over returns throttling responses. Longer prompts use up the quota faster, so trimming a bloated system message can relieve throttling as well as cost.

questions.prompt: An HR assistant must answer only from the company's current policy documents, which change every few weeks. Which approach should the team try first?
options: Fine-tune the base model on the policy documents
Add a system message and ground answers with retrieval over the documents
Raise the temperature so the model explores more answers
answer: Add a system message and ground answers with retrieval over the documents
questions.explain: Retrieval plus a clear system message is the cheap, fast option, and it handles documents that change: you re-index instead of re-training. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge in at training time, so every policy edit means another training run. A bigger model does not know your policies either.
questions.teach: There are two main ways to make a model answer from your own content. One is to retrain the model on it, called fine-tuning, which bakes the content into the model at training time. The other is to fetch the relevant passages at the moment of each question and put them in the prompt, together with instructions on how to use them. They differ sharply in cost, speed and how they handle content that keeps changing.
hints: The key detail is that the policy documents change every few weeks. Ask what each option would cost you every time a policy is edited: nothing, a quick refresh, or a whole new training run.

Baking knowledge into the model means every edit needs retraining, which is slow and costly for documents that change this often. The better approach reads the current documents at the time of each question.

Raising temperature makes answers more varied, not more accurate. The largest model still has never seen your policies. Pick the option that supplies the current documents plus rules for answering from them.
questions.deep: The drill's rule of thumb: try instructions plus retrieval first, and reach for fine-tuning when you need a fixed style or output format on every call and have many high-quality worked examples. With retrieval, a policy edit means re-indexing, not re-training.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps of a single retrieval-augmented request, from first to last.
tray: Insert the retrieved passages into the prompt
Turn the user's question into an embedding
Generate the grounded answer
Search the index for the closest passages
answer: Turn the user's question into an embedding
Search the index for the closest passages
Insert the retrieved passages into the prompt
Generate the grounded answer
questions.explain: The question is embedded, the index returns the nearest passages, those passages are added to the prompt as grounding data, and the model generates from that combined input. No training happens anywhere in this loop, which is what makes it cheap enough to run per request.
questions.teach: Retrieval-augmented generation answers a question from your own documents without retraining the model. The documents are stored in an index as embeddings, which are lists of numbers that capture meaning so that similar texts sit close together. At question time the system has to turn the question into the same kind of numbers before it can compare it with the index, and the model only sees what gets put in its prompt.
hints: The last step is the answer the user sees, so generation comes at the end. Work backwards from there: what must the model have in its prompt before it can write a grounded answer?
Searching an index of embeddings means comparing numbers with numbers. The question starts as words, so it has to be converted into an embedding before any search can happen.

Passages cannot be inserted into the prompt until the search has found them, and the model cannot use them until they are in the prompt. Line the steps up so each one uses what the previous one produced.
questions.deep: No training happens anywhere in this loop, which is what makes it cheap enough to run per request. The web drill adds a distractor step, retraining the model on the retrieved passages; that is fine-tuning, and it is the line the exam draws between the two.

questions.prompt: An assistant must look up a customer's live order status in an internal system while answering. Which capability lets the model do this?
options: Function calling, so the model can request a defined tool
answer: Function calling, so the model can request a defined tool
questions.explain: Function calling lets you describe tools to the model; the model then asks for one by name with arguments, your code runs it and returns the result. A bigger context window gives more room for text you already have, and fine-tuning on past orders would teach yesterday's data, not today's status.
questions.teach: A language model on its own can only produce text from what is in its prompt and what it learned in training. It cannot reach into live systems by itself. To connect it to live data, developers describe the available tools to the model, and the model can then ask for one, with arguments, when it needs it. The app runs the tool and sends the result back so the model can finish its answer.
hints: The word live is the clue. The order status changes by the minute and sits in an internal system. Ask which option lets the model get fresh information at the moment of the question.
More room in the prompt only helps with text you already have, and the status is not in the prompt. A higher temperature makes answers more varied, which does nothing to fetch data.
Training on past orders teaches yesterday's data, not today's status, and training takes time. The remaining option lets the model ask your code to run a lookup and hand back the current result.
questions.deep: With function calling the model never runs anything itself: it returns a tool name and arguments, your code executes the call, and you pass the result back. Scope each tool's permissions to exactly what it needs, because tools widen the blast radius of a wrong or manipulated answer.

questions.prompt: Six weeks after launch, an assistant's answers get noticeably worse because the underlying product documentation was rewritten. What should the team have had in place?
options: Continuous evaluation and monitoring of answer quality in production
answer: Continuous evaluation and monitoring of answer quality in production
questions.explain: Quality decays when the world behind the system changes, so evaluation is a standing process rather than a launch checkbox. Running the evaluation set on a schedule and watching groundedness in production is what surfaces the decay before users report it.
questions.teach: An AI system can be good on launch day and worse a month later without anyone changing its code, because the world behind it changes: documents are rewritten, products change, users ask new things. Testing therefore comes in two shapes. One is a check before release. The other is a standing process that keeps measuring quality after release, on a schedule, so decay shows up in the numbers before users report it.
hints: The system passed launch, then got worse six weeks later when the documentation changed. Ask which option would have noticed that change after launch, rather than only before it.
A single pre-release test pass is a snapshot. It says the system was fine on the day of the test, and nothing about what happens when the documents behind it get rewritten later.
Temperature changes randomness, and more training epochs would not help because nothing about the model changed; the content did. Pick the option that keeps measuring answer quality after release.
questions.deep: Evaluation is a standing process, not a launch checkbox. Running a fixed evaluation set on a schedule and watching groundedness in production surfaces decay early. The exam also tests the reverse: a manual spot-check is never a release gate.

questions.prompt: A team wants to remove the API key from application configuration entirely. Which approach should they use?
options: Store the key in an environment variable
Authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID using a managed identity
Base64-encode the key before storing it
answer: Authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID using a managed identity
questions.explain: A managed identity gives the application an identity in Microsoft Entra ID, so it requests a token at runtime and no key exists to leak. Environment variables, rotation and encoding all still keep a secret somewhere; only the keyless path removes it.
questions.teach: Apps prove to a service that they are allowed to use it in one of two ways. One is a shared secret such as an API key, which has to be stored somewhere and can leak from wherever it is stored. The other is an identity: the platform gives the app an identity in a directory, and the app asks for a short-lived token at runtime, so no long-lived secret sits in its configuration at all.
hints: The goal is to remove the key entirely, not to protect it better. Ask of each option: after this change, does a secret still exist somewhere that someone could steal?

An environment variable is still a place where the key sits. Rotating it every 30 days means a new key keeps existing. Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse, so the key is still there in a thin disguise.
Three options keep a secret and change how it is stored or refreshed. Only one option replaces the key with an identity that requests tokens when it runs, so there is nothing stored to leak.
questions.deep: Keyless authentication through Microsoft Entra ID with a managed identity is the exam's answer whenever a question says remove or eliminate keys. Base64 is a favourite distractor because it looks like protection but is only an encoding.

questions.prompt: A legal team wants an assistant that answers strictly from a fixed set of contract PDFs and refuses anything else. Which combination is the right build?
options: Index the PDFs, retrieve into the prompt, and instruct the model to refuse when the context does not cover the question
Fine-tune on the PDFs and remove the system message
Raise the temperature and add more few-shot examples
Deploy two models and average their answers
answer: Index the PDFs, retrieve into the prompt, and instruct the model to refuse when the context does not cover the question
questions.explain: Grounding supplies the content and the system message supplies the refusal rule; you need both, because retrieval alone will still let the model improvise when it finds nothing. Fine-tuning cannot be pointed at a fixed set of sources at answer time, and averaging two models does not create a boundary.
questions.teach: Keeping an assistant inside a fixed body of sources takes two ingredients. One supplies the right content: the relevant passages must reach the model at question time. The other sets the boundary: rules telling the model what to do when the supplied content does not answer the question. Content without rules lets the model improvise, and rules without content leave it nothing to answer from.
hints: The requirement has two halves: answer strictly from the contract PDFs, and refuse anything else. Look for the option that addresses both halves, not just one of them.

Fine-tuning bakes content into the model during training, and it cannot be pointed at a specific set of sources when a question arrives. Removing the system message also removes the only place to state a refusal rule.
Temperature and extra examples change style, and averaging two models does not create a boundary. One option supplies the content at question time and states what to do when that content falls short.
questions.deep: Retrieval alone still lets the model improvise when it finds nothing relevant, so the refusal instruction is part of the design, not an extra. Test with questions deliberately outside the contracts to confirm the refusal fires, and track groundedness in evaluation.

questions.prompt: Arrange the stages of shipping a grounded assistant, from first to last.
tray: Evaluate it against a fixed test set
Define the use case and how you will measure success
Monitor quality in production
Ground it with the organization's own content
Choose a model and deploy it
answer: Define the use case and how you will measure success
Choose a model and deploy it
Ground it with the organization's own content
Evaluate it against a fixed test set
Monitor quality in production
questions.explain: Measures come first, because everything downstream is judged against them. Model choice and grounding build the thing, evaluation decides whether it is good enough to release, and monitoring catches the decay that evaluation cannot predict.
questions.teach: Shipping an AI assistant follows a lifecycle, much like any product. You decide what success means, build the thing, check it against that definition before release, and keep checking after release, because quality can decay when the content or the users change. Skipping a stage usually shows up later as a problem nobody can measure.
hints: Ask what everything else is judged against. Evaluation and monitoring both need a definition of good, so the step that sets that definition has to come before anything is built.
You cannot ground a model that does not exist yet, so choosing and deploying a model comes before connecting it to your organization's content. Building comes before judging what you built.
Evaluating against a fixed test set decides whether the assistant is good enough to release. Monitoring watches it after release. The step that can only happen in production belongs at the very end.
questions.deep: Measures come first, because everything downstream is judged against them. Evaluation decides release; monitoring catches the decay evaluation cannot predict. The drill's distractor, releasing to all users before any evaluation, is the step the exam wants you to reject.

questions.prompt: Before choosing a model, a team wants to compare several large language models on quality and estimated cost in the Foundry portal. Where should they look?
options: The evaluation results of their own app
The model leaderboard in the model catalog
answer: The model leaderboard in the model catalog
questions.explain: The model leaderboard ranks catalog models on quality, safety, estimated cost and throughput, and its trade-off chart plots quality against cost. Content filters and quotas govern a deployment you already have, and your app's evaluations come after you have picked a model.
questions.teach: Choosing a model is a trade-off: the model with the best quality is rarely the cheapest or the fastest. Foundry separates tools for choosing a model from tools for running one. Before choosing, you compare candidates on measured quality, safety, estimated cost and throughput. After choosing, you set quotas and content filters on your deployment and evaluate the app you build on top of it.
hints: The team has not chosen a model yet, and wants to compare several on quality and cost. Any option that only exists once you have a deployment or an app answers a different question.
Content filters and quota pages both govern a deployment you already have. They say nothing about how one model's quality or price compares with another's.
Evaluating your own app happens after you have picked a model and built something with it. One option ranks catalog models side by side on quality and estimated cost before you commit.
questions.deep: The leaderboard's trade-off chart plots quality against cost, so you can see which model gives the most quality for the spend. On the exam, compare before choosing points to the catalog and leaderboard; judge after building points to evaluations.

questions.prompt: Responses from a deployed model must stay within a fixed length to keep costs down. Which parameter should you set?
answer: Max completion tokens
questions.explain: The completion-token cap sets a hard limit on reply length, and because output tokens are billed, it caps cost per call too. Temperature and top P change how the next word is picked, not how many are written, and the model version changes the model itself.
questions.teach: A model's output is billed by the token, so the length of a reply is also its cost. Some settings change how the model picks each next word, making replies more or less varied. Another setting puts a hard cap on how many tokens a reply may contain. Changing which model version you use changes the model itself. Each setting controls a different property, and length is controlled by only one of them.
hints: The requirement is a fixed length to control cost. Ask which option counts tokens in the reply, rather than changing which words are picked or which model does the picking.
Two options, temperature and top P, both shape randomness in the choice of next token. They change what is written, not how much, so a reply can be just as long at any value of either.

Swapping the model version changes the model, not a length limit, and a different version may even write longer answers. Only one option sets a hard ceiling on reply length, and through it on cost per call.
questions.deep: Because output tokens are billed, the completion-token cap is both a length limit and a cost limit per call. The exam's favourite distractor is temperature offered as a fix for length; temperature shapes variety, never size.

questions.prompt: A developer is writing prompts for a deployed chat model. Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: Few-shot examples placed in the prompt change the model's weights
Asking the model to work through the steps can improve answers to multi-step problems
A system message guarantees the model will never produce unwanted output
A system message sets the assistant's role and the rules it should follow
answer: Asking the model to work through the steps can improve answers to multi-step problems
A system message sets the assistant's role and the rules it should follow
questions.explain: The system message steers role and rules, and prompting the model to reason step by step is a documented technique for multi-step problems. Few-shot examples teach within one request only and train nothing, and a system message is instruction, not enforcement, which is why content filters exist as a separate layer.
questions.teach: Prompt engineering changes what the model reads, never the model itself. The system message sets the role, tone and rules. Few-shot examples show the pattern you want inside the same request. Asking for step-by-step reasoning helps on problems with several steps. None of these is a hard guarantee.
