hints: Sort the statements into two groups: those claiming a prompt changes the model permanently or guarantees an outcome, and those claiming a prompt steers the model's behaviour.
Ask what happens to few-shot examples after the request ends. If nothing is trained, the model has forgotten them on the next call, so its weights cannot have changed.
A determined user can argue with a system message. That is why content filtering exists as a separate control, so any statement promising never should be treated with suspicion.
questions.deep: Exam pattern: prompts steer and filters enforce. Words like guarantees, never and always in a prompt-engineering statement usually mark it false. Few-shot is sometimes called in-context learning, and the context part is the clue that it is temporary.

questions.prompt: A team is setting up evaluation for a grounded assistant. Which three statements are true? Choose three.
options: Evaluations can be re-run on a fixed dataset every time the prompt changes
Groundedness measures whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context
One manual spot-check of a few answers is enough to sign off a production release
Relevance measures whether the answer addresses the question that was asked
answer: Evaluations can be re-run on a fixed dataset every time the prompt changes
Groundedness measures whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context
Relevance measures whether the answer addresses the question that was asked
questions.explain: Groundedness and relevance are distinct: an answer can be perfectly grounded in a passage that has nothing to do with the question. Manual spot-checks help early but are not a release gate. Re-running a fixed evaluation set on every prompt change is the point of automated evaluation, because prompt edits regress quietly.
questions.teach: Foundry offers built-in evaluators for generative apps. Groundedness asks whether each claim in the answer is backed by the retrieved context. Relevance asks whether the answer responds to the actual question. Others cover coherence, fluency and safety. You run them over a fixed test set so that results are comparable between versions.
hints: Two statements define metrics. Check each definition carefully: one metric compares the answer with the context, the other compares the answer with the question.
Ask whether a handful of answers checked by hand could catch a problem that only affects one kind of question in twenty. That tells you whether spot-checks are enough for release.
A fixed dataset means the same questions every time, so any change in scores comes from your change. That is exactly how you catch a prompt edit that quietly makes things worse.
questions.deep: Grounded but irrelevant, and relevant but ungrounded, are both real failure modes, which is why the two metrics are separate. Foundry can run evaluations in bulk on a dataset and continuously on production traffic.

questions.prompt: A team is deploying an agent that can act on behalf of users. Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: An agent's tools should run with full administrator permissions to avoid errors
Giving an agent tools removes the need to check what it produces
Conversation state lets an agent use earlier turns as context
An agent can be given tools it may call to fetch data or take actions
answer: Conversation state lets an agent use earlier turns as context
An agent can be given tools it may call to fetch data or take actions
questions.explain: Tools extend what an agent can do and widen the damage it can cause at the same time, so its credentials should be scoped to exactly what it needs. Nothing about tool use removes the need for evaluation and monitoring; tools raise the stakes of skipping them.
questions.teach: An agent is a model plus instructions plus tools plus memory of the conversation. Tools let it call functions, search data or act in other systems. Conversation state, called a thread, lets it remember earlier turns. Because an agent can act, security rules such as least privilege matter more than they do for a plain chat model.
hints: Two statements describe what agents are made of. Two others make claims about safety shortcuts. Test each shortcut by asking what would happen if the agent made a mistake.
If an agent's tool runs as administrator and the model misreads an instruction, what is the worst it could do? That tells you how to judge the permissions statement.
Tools let an agent do more, which means a wrong output can now cause a real action. Ask whether that makes checking its output more or less important.
questions.deep: Least privilege, managed identity, human approval for risky actions and continuous evaluation are the standard agent controls. Foundry Agent Service stores conversation state in threads and lets you attach tools such as file search, code interpreter and your own functions.

questions.prompt: A team is deciding which planned features need an agent and which need only a single call to a generative model. Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: Rewriting one paragraph in a friendlier tone needs an agent
An assistant that must look up an employee's ticket and then open a new one in the helpdesk system is a good fit for an agent with tools
Summarizing an email the user pastes in needs only a single model call
An agent must be fine-tuned before it can use tools
answer: An assistant that must look up an employee's ticket and then open a new one in the helpdesk system is a good fit for an agent with tools
Summarizing an email the user pastes in needs only a single model call
questions.explain: An agent earns its place when a job takes several steps, calls tools or systems, and keeps state between turns. One-shot text jobs such as rewriting or summarizing need only a prompt and a response. Agents get their tools through configuration and instructions, with no fine-tuning involved.
questions.teach: Not every AI feature needs an agent. A single model call takes a prompt and returns text, which is enough for rewriting, summarizing or classifying something the user provides. An agent adds tools, several steps and memory, and is worth that extra complexity when the job must look things up or change things in other systems.
hints: For each feature, ask whether it needs anything beyond the text the user provides. If everything needed is already in the prompt, a single call is enough.
The helpdesk feature must read one system and then write to another. Ask how a model could do that without being given tools.
Tools are attached to an agent through its configuration. Ask whether fine-tuning, which changes a model's weights, has anything to do with giving it access to a function.
questions.deep: The agentic AI workload is new on AI-901. Look for scenario words like look up, then do, across systems, or on the user's behalf. Plain transform-this-text jobs are generative AI without agents and cost less and fail less.

questions.prompt: Which two situations point towards fine-tuning a model rather than using retrieval? Choose two.
options: You have a large set of high-quality example inputs and outputs
You need answers about documents that change daily
You want every answer to cite the source passage it came from
You need the model to follow a very specific output format or house style on every call
answer: You have a large set of high-quality example inputs and outputs
You need the model to follow a very specific output format or house style on every call
questions.explain: Fine-tuning teaches behaviour and style from many worked examples, and those examples must exist. Fast-changing content and citations are retrieval's job, because retrieval reads the document at request time and can point at it.
questions.teach: Fine-tuning and retrieval solve different problems. Fine-tuning trains a model further on many example conversations so that it reliably adopts a style, format or behaviour. Retrieval leaves the model alone and gives it fresh facts inside the prompt. A useful short version: fine-tune for how it answers, retrieve for what it knows.
hints: Sort the four situations into 'how the model should answer' and 'what facts the model needs'. Fine-tuning mainly changes the first of these.
If documents change every day, a model trained last week is already out of date. Ask which approach reads the latest version at the moment of the question.
Citations need to point to a specific passage the answer came from. Fine-tuned knowledge is blended into weights and has no passage to point at.
questions.deep: Fine-tuning is expensive and needs hundreds of good examples. Microsoft's guidance is to try prompt engineering, then RAG, and only then fine-tuning. The approaches combine: a fine-tuned model can still use RAG.

questions.prompt: A developer has deployed a chat model in Foundry and tested it in the playground. Which two items does a small Python app need before it can send prompts to that deployment? Choose two.
options: The dataset the model was trained on
The display name of the Foundry project
A credential: an API key or a Microsoft Entra ID identity
The endpoint of the project or deployment
answer: A credential: an API key or a Microsoft Entra ID identity
The endpoint of the project or deployment
questions.explain: A client needs to know where to send the request, which is the endpoint, and how to prove it is allowed to, which is a key or an Entra ID token. The deployment name is passed as the model in each call. Playground history, training data and the display name play no part in calling the model.
questions.teach: Every call to a cloud AI service answers two questions: where does the request go, and who is asking? The endpoint answers the first; it is the URL of your Foundry project or resource. A credential answers the second: either an API key or a token from Microsoft Entra ID. With those two and the deployment name, the SDK can make the call.
hints: Think of posting a letter: you need an address, and something that proves you are allowed to send it. Look for the two options that play those two roles.
The playground chat history is a record of your testing. The app does not need to replay your old conversations to send a new prompt.
Training data stays with whoever trained the model, and a display name is just a label in the portal. Neither is used to reach or authenticate to the deployment.
questions.deep: In the Foundry SDK you create a client from the project endpoint and a credential such as DefaultAzureCredential, then pass the deployment name as the model parameter. Entra ID with a managed identity avoids storing keys at all.

questions.prompt: You are creating an agent in Microsoft Foundry that must take on a specific role and behave in a set way when it responds to users. What should you configure?
answer: System instructions
questions.explain: An agent's instructions define its role, tone, rules and what it should refuse. Temperature controls randomness, TPM is a throughput quota, and max completion tokens caps reply length.
questions.teach: When you create an agent in the Foundry portal you give it a model, instructions and optional tools. The instructions are a system message written in plain language: who the agent is, how it should speak, what it may and may not do. Numeric settings tune how it generates text but cannot describe a role.
hints: A role and a way of behaving are described in words. Ask which option lets you write sentences telling the agent who it is and how to act.
Temperature is a number that changes how varied the wording is. A number cannot tell the agent it is a polite travel assistant.
TPM and max completion tokens are limits on throughput and length. They control how much, not how, so leave the option where you describe the behaviour.
questions.deep: The exam likes to offer parameters as answers to behaviour questions. Behaviour and role go in instructions, randomness in temperature or top-p, length and cost in max tokens, throughput in TPM quota. Learn that four-way split and several items become easy.

questions.prompt: What are two purposes of the instructions you give a generative AI model or agent? Choose two.
options: Set the Azure region where inference runs
Define the agent's role and behaviour
Define constraints on the model's responses
Set the tokens-per-minute allocation for the model
Choose which model the request is sent to
answer: Define the agent's role and behaviour
Define constraints on the model's responses
questions.explain: Instructions say who the model is, how it behaves and what limits its answers must respect, such as topics to refuse or a required format. Model choice, region and TPM are deployment settings configured outside the prompt.
questions.teach: Instructions, also called the system prompt, are text the model reads before every user message. They can set a persona, a tone, a scope, rules to follow and the format of answers. They cannot change infrastructure: which model runs, where it runs and how much traffic it may take are decided when you create the deployment.
hints: Ask which options could be written as a sentence to the model, such as 'you are a support agent' or 'answer only about billing'. Those are what instructions can do.
The model, the region and the traffic quota are all chosen when the deployment is created in Azure. A sentence in the prompt cannot move a deployment to another region.
That leaves one option about identity and behaviour and one about limits on the answers. Both are things the model reads and follows.
questions.deep: On AI-901, 'create effective system and user prompts' is an explicit skill. Good instructions state a role, a scope, output format and a fallback, such as saying you do not know when the context lacks the answer. That fallback is also a grounding control.

questions.prompt: You plan to deploy a model from the Foundry model catalog so that it runs on dedicated virtual machines hosted for your project. Which deployment option should you use?
answer: Managed compute
questions.explain: Managed compute deploys the model to dedicated virtual machines that Azure manages for you, and you pay for the VM hours. A serverless API runs the model on shared Microsoft-hosted capacity with pay-per-token billing and no VMs of your own. AKS and raw VMs would mean hosting the model yourself outside Foundry's deployment options.
questions.teach: Foundry offers two main ways to deploy catalog models. Serverless, also called standard or pay-as-you-go, means Microsoft hosts the model on shared infrastructure and you pay per token. Managed compute means Foundry provisions dedicated virtual machines for your deployment and you pay for them while they run, whether or not they are busy.
hints: The key word is dedicated. Ask which deployment option gives your model its own machines instead of sharing Microsoft's.
Serverless means you never see or pay for machines; you pay per token on shared capacity. That is the opposite of dedicated virtual machines.
Kubernetes clusters and plain virtual machines would mean building the hosting yourself, outside Foundry's deployment choices. One option is Foundry's own managed dedicated-VM choice.
questions.deep: One practice video marks serverless API as the answer here, which contradicts Microsoft's documentation. Serverless is pay-per-token on Microsoft-hosted capacity, and managed compute is dedicated VMs billed per hour. Some models are offered only one way.

questions.prompt: In a Foundry project, a gpt-4.1-mini model is deployed on the resource contoso-ai under the deployment name support-bot. An app calls it with the OpenAI Python client pointed at that resource. What should the model argument be?
questions.code:
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=key,
    base_url="https://contoso-ai.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/",
)
response = client.responses.create(
    model=____,
    input="Hello",
)
answer: "support-bot"
questions.explain: On Azure you call a deployment, so the model argument carries the deployment name, which routes the request to that deployment's settings and quota. The resource name goes in the endpoint URL, and the base model name alone does not identify which deployment to use.
questions.teach: In Azure, you never call a base model directly. You first create a deployment: a named instance of a model with its own version, quota and filters. Code then talks to the resource's endpoint URL and names the deployment in each request. Two deployments of the same model can have different settings, which is why the name matters.
hints: Three names appear in the scenario: the resource, the model and the deployment. Ask which one is already used in the endpoint URL, and which is left to identify the target.
The same base model could be deployed twice on one resource with different quotas or filters. Ask which name lets a request pick between those two.
On Azure the model argument names the thing you created in the portal, not the catalog entry you created it from.
questions.deep: With the OpenAI SDK against Azure, the base_url is https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/ and model= takes the deployment name. The exam likes to offer the base model name as a distractor, because on the public OpenAI API that name would be right.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about a model deployed in Foundry are true? Choose two.
options: Temperature must be chosen during deployment and cannot change afterwards
Temperature is set on each request or in the playground, not fixed when the model is deployed
The base model name routes each request to the right deployment
After deployment you can use the model both from code and from testing tools such as the playground
answer: Temperature is set on each request or in the playground, not fixed when the model is deployed
After deployment you can use the model both from code and from testing tools such as the playground
questions.explain: Temperature is an inference parameter sent with each request, so it can change call by call. A deployment is reachable from the playground and from SDK code alike. Requests are routed by deployment name, because the same base model can have several deployments.
questions.teach: Deployment settings and request settings are different things. When you deploy, you pick the model, version, deployment name, deployment type and quota. Each request then carries its own parameters, such as temperature, top-p and max tokens. That split lets one deployment serve both a creative feature and a precise one.
hints: Sort the statements into deployment-time settings and per-request settings. Ask which group temperature belongs to by thinking about whether two calls could use different values.
Once a model is deployed, the playground and your Python code both talk to the same endpoint. Ask whether anything would stop you using both.
If two deployments of the same base model exist, the base model's name cannot say which one you meant. Something more specific must do the routing.
questions.deep: Deployment time fixes model, version, name, type (standard, global, provisioned) and TPM quota. Request time sets messages or input, temperature, top_p, max tokens, tools and tool_choice. Exam statements that move a request parameter into deployment time are false.

questions.prompt: An agent in Foundry has one function tool that looks up order status. It must call a tool every time it responds, never answering from the model alone. What should tool_choice be set to?
answer: "required"
questions.explain: tool_choice="required" forces the model to call at least one tool on every turn. "auto" lets the model decide, which is the default, "none" forbids tool calls, and "parallel" is not a tool_choice value.
questions.teach: When a model has tools, tool_choice controls whether it uses them. With auto, the model decides for itself whether a tool is needed. With none, it may not call tools. With required, it must call a tool. You can also name one specific function to force that exact tool.
hints: The requirement says the agent must use a tool every time it responds. Ask which setting takes away the model's freedom to skip its tools.
auto is the default and leaves the decision to the model, which means it might sometimes answer without calling anything. That breaks the every-time rule.
none is the opposite of what is needed. Of the remaining options, only one is a real tool_choice value, and its name says a call must happen.
questions.deep: Forcing a tool on every turn can loop, because the model must call a tool even after it has the answer. Common practice is to force the first call, then switch back to auto. You can also force a specific function by passing its name instead of "required".

questions.prompt: Match each setting to the job it does when an app calls a deployed model.
options: Sets the assistant's role and rules
Controls how random the word choice is
Caps how long, and so how costly, each reply can be
Makes the model callable by name from an app
answer: Sets the assistant's role and rules
Controls how random the word choice is
Caps how long, and so how costly, each reply can be
Makes the model callable by name from an app
questions.explain: Instructions shape behaviour, temperature shapes variety, the token cap shapes length and therefore cost, and a deployment is the named, callable instance of a model. The exam likes to offer one of these as the answer to a question about another, most often temperature as a fix for length.
questions.teach: A request to a language model carries more than the user's question. Some settings steer what the model is told, some steer how it picks words, and some limit size. Text is counted in tokens, small chunks of a word, and replies are limited and billed by token count. The model writes one token at a time by choosing among likely candidates, and a setting can make that choice strict or loose. Cloud platforms also expect you to set a model up before your code can reach it.
hints: Each row is a setting, and each option describes a job. Take the rows one at a time and say aloud what you would expect to change if you altered that setting. Some settings change what the model is told, some change how it samples words, some change size, and one is about access.

Two rows give strong clues. One is about tokens, the unit that replies are counted and billed in, and one is about randomness, which links to how the model picks among likely next words. Match those two first and the remaining pair becomes much easier to separate.

For the remaining two, ask which one is text you write to give the assistant a persona and boundaries, and which one is an object you create on the platform before any code can reach the model. Remember that a setting for variety does not control reply length, which is a common trap.
questions.deep: Temperature and top_p both reshape the next-token distribution, so tune one at a time. A max token cap truncates a reply rather than making it concise, so ask for brevity in the instructions too. Reasoning models may fix or reject the temperature setting.

questions.prompt: What does len("hello") return?
questions.explain: len() returns the number of items in a container; for a string that is the number of characters, so "hello" gives 5. There is no off-by-one for the terminating character, because Python strings do not use one.
questions.teach:
len() is a built in function that counts how many items a container holds. Give it a list and it counts the elements; give it a string and it counts the characters, including spaces and punctuation. It counts the way you would count things on a shelf, starting from one, unlike index positions, which start from zero.
nums = [10, 20, 30]
len(nums)   # 3
len("a b")  # 3, the space counts too
hints: Think about what len stands for: length. It asks how many things are inside whatever you hand it. Here the thing is a piece of text in quotes, so the question becomes how many characters make it up.

Count the letters one at a time, touching a finger on each as you go, and start your count at one. Ignore the quotation marks, because they only tell Python that this is text and are not part of the string itself.

Two of the wrong options come from counting mistakes: one is a letter short and one adds something that is not there, as if the text ended with a hidden extra character. The last wrong option claims an error, but len happily accepts strings. Your own careful count of the letters is the answer.
questions.deep: len() calls the object's __len__ method, so it is constant time for str, list and dict because the size is stored, not counted. For strings it counts Unicode code points, not bytes or visible glyphs: an accented letter built from a base letter plus a combining mark counts as 2.

questions.prompt: Which expression creates a dictionary?
questions.explain: Curly braces with colon-separated pairs create a dict. Square brackets make a list and parentheses make a tuple. The trap is the last one: curly braces without colons create a set, so {"a", 1} is a two-element set, not a mapping.
questions.teach:
A dictionary stores pairs, where each key is a label and each value is the thing filed under that label. You look things up by key instead of by position, like finding a phone number by searching for a name. Python has several collection types, such as lists, tuples and sets, and each one has its own written form so that Python can tell which one you mean. Once a dictionary exists, you read from it like this:
phone["Sam"]
which hands back whatever is filed under the key "Sam".
hints: This question is about how Python tells collections apart by the brackets and symbols you write. Think about what makes a dictionary special: every entry is a pair made of a key and a value, so the written form needs some mark that links the two halves of each entry.

Look at each option and ask two things: which kind of bracket does it use, and is each entry a single loose item or a linked pair? Square brackets and round brackets already belong to two other well known collections, so you can set those two options aside.

Two options are left, and they use the same kind of bracket, so the brackets alone will not settle it. The difference is one small symbol. Pick the option where something sits between the two pieces of the entry to link a key with its value, rather than the one that just lists loose items separated by commas.
questions.deep: Curly braces are shared by dict and set literals, and the colon is what decides between them. A classic trap is that {} on its own is an empty dict, not an empty set, so use set() for that. Dict keys must be hashable, which is why a list cannot be a key but a tuple of hashable items can.

questions.prompt: What does print(type([])) output?
answer: <class 'list'>
questions.explain: type() returns the type object, and printing it shows the  form. Python has no built-in type called array; the built-in sequence type is list.
questions.teach:
Every value in Python has a type, and the built in function type() tells you which one. The answer is itself an object, so print shows it in a fixed text format rather than as a bare word. Try it on a piece of text:
print(type("hi"))
This prints <class 'str'>, which reads as: the class named str. The name inside the quotes is the name of the type. Note that type() reports what a value is, not what it looks like when you write it.
hints: Two separate ideas meet in this question. First, what kind of thing does type() give back, and how does print display it? Second, what is the name Python uses for the value written with square brackets and nothing inside? Work out each idea on its own, then combine them.

Remember the format shown earlier: the word class, then the type's name in quotes, all wrapped in angle brackets. Now think about the name itself. Python's everyday ordered collection that you can change has a short, plain name, and it is not the word that some other languages use for a similar thing.

Rule out the options that print only a bare name or only the brackets, since print shows a type object in the angle bracket form you saw earlier. Two options remain, and one of them uses a type name that Python does not have as a built in. Choose the other one, the name of the type behind a square bracket collection.
questions.deep: type(x) returns the class object, and print calls str() on it, which for classes gives the <class '...'> form. In real code prefer isinstance(x, list) over type(x) == list so subclasses still match. The array module and numpy arrays exist, but neither is the type of the literal [].

questions.prompt: What happens when you evaluate "3" + 3?
answer: It raises a TypeError
questions.explain: Python does not coerce between str and int for +, so mixing them raises TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. You have to say which you meant: int("3") + 3 gives 6, and "3" + str(3) gives "33".
questions.teach:
Quotes turn something into text, even if it looks like a number. The text "3" is a character, while the number 3 is a value you can do arithmetic with. The + sign has two jobs: with two numbers it adds, and with two pieces of text it joins them end to end.
2 + 2 gives 4
"a" + "b" gives "ab"
Both jobs work when the two sides are the same kind of thing. What happens when the two sides are different kinds is worth thinking through before you run it.
hints: Start by looking at the two sides of the plus sign and asking what kind of value each one is. One of them has quotes around it and one does not. The question is whether Python treats those as the same kind of thing, and what it does when asked to combine two different kinds.

Python gives plus two jobs: adding numbers and joining text. Neither job makes sense with one of each. Some languages quietly convert one side so the line works anyway, but Python prefers to make you decide. Think about which style Python follows here, guess and convert, or stop and complain.

Several options suggest that Python quietly produced some value, either a number or a piece of text. Ask yourself whether Python would pick which of those two conversions you wanted without being told. If it refuses to guess, no value comes out at all, and something else happens instead of a result.
questions.deep: Python is strongly typed: it will not silently convert between str and int, whereas JavaScript would quietly give "33" here. Convert on purpose with int(), str() or an f-string so the intent is visible. Note that "3" * 3 does work, because it means repeat the text.

questions.prompt: Given nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], what is nums[1:4]?
questions.explain: Slices start at the first index and stop before the second, so 1:4 takes positions 1, 2 and 3. Indexing starts at 0, which is why the result begins at 2 and not at 1.
questions.teach:
Positions in a list are counted from zero, so the first item sits at position 0, the second at position 1, and so on. A slice copies a stretch of the list, written start:stop inside square brackets. The slice begins at the start position and runs up to, but not including, the stop position.
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]
letters[0:2]
This picks positions 0 and 1, so the result is ["a", "b"].
hints: Before slicing, write the list out with its positions underneath each item, starting your count at zero rather than one. The numbers 1 and 4 in the brackets are positions, not values, so you first need to know which item sits at each position.

A slice has a start and a stop. The start position is included. The stop position works differently from what many people expect: Python stops just before reaching it. Mark where the slice begins and where it stops, and keep only the items between those two marks.

Check each option by looking at its first item and its last item. The first item must be the one sitting at position 1, which is not the very first item of the list. The last item must be the one just before position 4. Also, the number of items should equal stop minus start.
questions.deep: A slice is a half-open interval, so len(nums[a:b]) is b - a and nums[:k] + nums[k:] rebuilds the list with no gap or overlap. Slices make a shallow copy and never raise IndexError for out-of-range bounds; they just clamp.

questions.prompt: Which three statements are true? Choose three.
options: An empty list is falsy in a boolean test
Strings are mutable, so s[0] = "x" works
is compares identity while == compares value
A tuple can be used as a dictionary key
answer: An empty list is falsy in a boolean test
is compares identity while == compares value
A tuple can be used as a dictionary key
questions.explain: Empty containers, 0 and None are falsy. Strings are immutable, so you build a new one instead of editing in place. is asks whether two names point at the same object, which is why it is the wrong tool for comparing numbers or strings. Tuples are hashable when their contents are, so they work as keys where lists do not.
questions.teach: This question mixes four small ideas. Truthiness: in an if, Python can judge any value as yes or no, and a few values count as no while most count as yes. Mutability: some objects can be edited in place, others never change once made. Identity versus equality: two names can hold equal content yet be two separate objects, and Python has a separate tool for each question. Hashing: a dictionary finds its keys by a fixed fingerprint, so a key's fingerprint must never change. Try bool(0) in the REPL to see truthiness at work.
hints: Judge each statement on its own as true or false before comparing them. Exactly three are true and one is false, so you are really hunting for the single false statement. Picture typing each claim into a Python prompt and ask what would actually happen.

The false statement is about changing something in place. Think about what happens if you try to assign to a single character of a piece of text: does Python edit it, or does it complain? Compare that with a list, where assigning to one position is perfectly fine.

Now confirm the other three. Python has one tool that asks whether two names are the very same object and another that asks whether their contents match. Containers holding nothing count as no in a yes or no test. And a key needs a fingerprint that never changes, which an object you can edit in place cannot promise.
questions.deep: Falsy values are None, False, zero of any numeric type, and empty str, list, tuple, dict, set and range. Use is only for singletons like None; small-int caching makes is seem to work on numbers, which is a CPython detail. A tuple is hashable only if all its items are, so (1, [2]) fails as a key.

questions.prompt: Given name = "Ada", what does f"Hi {name}" produce?
answer: Hi Ada
questions.explain: An f-string evaluates each brace expression and substitutes the result, so you get Hi Ada. Without the f prefix the braces stay literal, which is the usual reason this appears not to work.
questions.teach:
A normal string is just text, and Python copies every character as it is. An f-string is a string with the letter f right before its opening quote, and that letter switches on a feature: anything inside curly braces is treated as a small piece of Python code, evaluated, and the result is placed into the text. Example with a different value:
print(f"{2 + 3} apples")
This shows 5 apples, because 2 + 3 was worked out first and then dropped into the text.
hints: Look closely at what comes before the opening quote and at what sits inside the curly braces. Both details matter. Ask yourself what that leading letter tells Python to do with the braces, and what the name inside them refers to.

Inside the braces is a name, and the line above the question has already given that name a value. Python looks the name up and swaps the braces and everything in them for that value, turned into text. Nothing else in the string is touched, so the words around the braces stay exactly as typed.

Read the options with that in mind. One option leaves the braces and the name untouched, which would only happen without the special prefix. One keeps the letter f and the quote marks as if they were part of the text, which they are not. One claims the name does not exist, but it was defined.
questions.deep: f-strings are compiled into a join of the literal pieces and formatted values, so they are faster than % formatting or str.format. They accept format specs like f"{x:.2f}", and f"{x=}" prints both the expression and its value, which is handy for debugging.

questions.prompt: Which line defines a function whose second parameter has a default value?
answer: def f(a, b = 2):
questions.explain: Defaults are written with = in the parameter list. A colon there would be an annotation, not a default, Python uses def rather than function, and there is no default keyword.
questions.teach:
A function can be written so that some of its inputs are optional. You do that in the def line by giving a parameter a fallback value, which Python uses whenever the caller leaves that argument out. Think of a coffee order where sugar is assumed to be none unless you ask.
greet('Ada')
greet('Ada', 'Hello')
If greet was written that way, both calls are legal: the first uses the fallback and the second overrides it. Parameters without a fallback are required, and Python insists they come first.
hints: This question is about optional inputs to a function. Read every option and check how it begins, because only one word is the one Python uses to start defining a function, and a line that starts differently cannot be valid whatever follows.

Next look inside the brackets. Python has a plain symbol for attaching a value to a name, the same one you use in a line like x = 5. A different symbol in a parameter list is used for a note about what kind of value is expected, so it does not supply a fallback.

Two options can be dropped on grammar alone: one begins with a word Python does not use for functions, and another invents an extra word inside the parameter list that Python does not have. Of the two that remain, choose the one where b is simply given its value, the way a variable would be.
questions.deep: A default value is evaluated once, when the def statement runs, not on every call. That makes b=[] a classic trap, because every call shares one list. Use None as the default and build the list inside the function. PEP 8 writes b=2 without spaces, but b: int = 2 with spaces once there is an annotation.

questions.prompt: Arrange the clauses of a full try statement in the order Python requires.
tray: except
try
else
finally
answer: try
except
else
finally
questions.explain: The order is fixed: try, then except, then the optional else which runs only when no exception was raised, then finally which runs either way. Python spells the handler except; catch belongs to other languages.
questions.teach: Programs fail sometimes: a file is missing, a number is mistyped. A try statement lets you plan for that. One clause holds the risky code. Another clause is the handler that takes over if an error is raised, and you name the kind of error it deals with. An optional clause holds code that should run only when nothing went wrong. A cleanup clause holds work such as closing a file and runs whatever happened. Python is strict about how these parts are arranged, and a wrong arrangement is a SyntaxError.
hints: Think of the story of a risky action: you attempt something, something may go wrong, and afterwards you tidy up. Each of the four words names one part of that story. Start by asking which word has to open the whole statement, because nothing else can exist before it.

The handler clause exists to deal with whatever the guarded code raises, so it belongs right beside that code. The success-only clause only makes sense once the handlers have had their chance, so it waits behind them. Place those three pieces and see which one is left over.

The cleanup clause is promised to run in every case, whether things succeeded or failed, so it cannot be tucked into the middle of the others. Once the other three are in place, ask where a clause that always runs regardless of the outcome naturally belongs.
questions.deep: The cleanup clause runs even after a return, a break or an unhandled exception, so it is the place for releasing resources, though a with statement usually does that job better. Keep the guarded body tiny: errors raised in the success clause are not covered by the handlers, so they are never swallowed by accident.

questions.prompt: What does [x * 2 for x in range(3)] evaluate to?
questions.explain: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2, and the comprehension doubles each one, giving [0, 2, 4]. range starts at 0 and stops before its argument, which is the half of this most people get wrong.
questions.teach:
A list comprehension builds a new list in one line: an expression, then a for clause that supplies values, all inside square brackets. It replaces a loop that creates an empty list and appends to it.
words = [w.upper() for w in ['a', 'b']]
# words is ['A', 'B']
The expression runs once for every value the for clause supplies. The built in range produces a run of whole numbers to loop over, and you can always see exactly which ones with list(range(4)) in the interpreter.
hints: Break the expression into two parts: the for clause on the right, which decides what values x takes, and the expression on the left, which decides what goes into the list. Work out the values first, then apply the expression to each one.

The tricky part is range. Ask yourself two questions: what is the very first number it produces, and does the number inside the brackets ever appear in its output? Many learners guess that counting starts at one and ends on the given number, so test that guess honestly.

Once you know the values x will take, there should be exactly as many of them as the number inside the brackets. Double each one, keeping the order. Then look for the option with the right length whose smallest entry is twice the smallest value x can be.
questions.deep: range and slices share a half open convention: the start is included, the stop is not, so range(a, b) holds exactly b - a numbers and neighbouring ranges join without overlap. A comprehension also keeps x in its own scope, so it never leaks out.

questions.prompt: Match each Python operator to what it does.
answer: Floor division
Remainder
Exponent
Not equal
Membership test
questions.explain: // divides and discards the fractional part, % gives what is left over, ** raises to a power, != is inequality, and in tests membership. A single = is assignment and never a comparison, which is why Python rejects it inside an if condition instead of silently assigning.
questions.teach:
Operators are the little symbols or words that tell Python what to do with the values on either side. Arithmetic operators such as + and - give back a number. Comparison operators such as > and == give back True or False. Some operators are spelled as words, for example and, or and not. Reading code fluently means knowing each one on sight, including those that look like a doubled or altered version of a familiar symbol.
print(7 + 2)  # 9
print(7 > 2)  # True
hints: Five rows need partners and there are six choices, so exactly one choice will stay unused. Start with the rows you are most sure of and cross each choice off as you use it. Leaving the hardest rows until last makes them easy by elimination.

Group the choices by family. Several are arithmetic, one is a comparison that answers yes or no, and one asks whether something is contained in a collection. Two rows are doubled up versions of everyday symbols, and the doubling changes the meaning: one is related to division and the other to multiplication.

Picture dividing 7 sweets between 3 children: one operator tells you how many whole sweets each child gets, another tells you how many are left over on the table. The doubled star is repeated multiplication, like squaring. The leftover choice is the one that stores a value, and none of the rows does that.
questions.deep: // rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero, so -7 // 2 is -4, and % takes the sign of the right operand so that a == (a // b) * b + a % b always holds. C truncates toward zero instead. divmod(a, b) returns both results at once.

questions.prompt: Given d = {"a": 1}, what does d.get("b", 0) return?
questions.explain: get() returns the default you pass when the key is missing, so you get 0. Calling d["b"] instead would raise KeyError, and get() with no default returns None rather than raising.
questions.teach:
A dictionary stores values under labels called keys. You read one with square brackets, or with the method get:
d = {'x': 5}
print(d['x'])
print(d.get('x'))
Both show 5 because the key exists. The two ways only behave differently when the key is absent, and that difference is the whole reason get exists. The method also accepts an optional second argument, which the Python docs call default.
hints: Start by noticing that the dictionary holds only one key, a, while the question asks about a different key, b. So this is a lookup of a missing key, not an ordinary one. The whole question is what get does in that situation.

Read the second argument carefully: it is there for exactly this moment. Ask yourself why a method would bother to accept a spare value as input if it never used it. Also notice that get is a method call with parentheses, not a square bracket lookup, and that changes how a missing key is handled.

Compare get with its bracket cousin: a bracket lookup of a missing key stops the program, while get is designed to avoid that and hand you something instead. With one argument it hands back Python's own empty value, and with two it hands back the one you chose. Decide which of those cases this call is.
questions.deep: d.get(k, default) never inserts the key. To insert as well, use d.setdefault(k, v) or collections.defaultdict. Note that the default argument is evaluated eagerly even when the key exists, so d.get(k, expensive()) always pays for the call.

questions.prompt: Which two loops correctly visit every key and its value in a dict d?
options: for k in d: v = d[k]
for v in d.values(): k = d[v]
answer: for k, v in d.items():
for k in d: v = d[k]
questions.explain: items() yields (key, value) pairs, so it unpacks into two names. Iterating the dict directly yields keys, which you can then look up. Unpacking d itself fails because iterating a dict gives you one key at a time, not a pair, and the last option looks up a value as if it were a key.
questions.teach:
A for loop takes whatever it is walking through and hands you one item per step. If each item is a pair, you can unpack it into two names right in the loop line:
for name, score in [('Ann', 3), ('Bo', 5)]:
    print(name, score)
A dictionary stores pairs of key and value, and it can be walked through in a few different ways, each handing your loop a different kind of item. Before you pick a loop, ask what one step of it actually gives you, and test it by printing.
hints: Two of the four lines are correct, so check each one on its own rather than comparing them against each other. For each line, ask what one step of the loop hands over, and whether the names on the left can actually receive it.

Remember that a plain loop over a dictionary, with no method call, gives one thing per step and not a pair. A line that tries to split each step into two names will therefore struggle. Also check which lines have both a key and a value in hand by the time the body runs.

One correct line asks the dictionary for its pairs and unpacks them. The other takes a single item from the loop and uses it to fetch the matching value in the body. Among the wrong lines, watch for the one that treats a value as though it were a key, which only works by luck.
questions.deep: Iterating a dict yields keys, in insertion order since Python 3.7. Prefer items() over d[k] inside the loop: it skips a hash lookup per key and reads more clearly. Never add or remove keys while looping, which raises RuntimeError; loop over list(d) when you must.

questions.prompt: What is the bug in def add_item(item, basket=[]): basket.append(item); return basket?
options: The default list is created once at definition time and shared by every call
append() returns None, so the function returns nothing
Lists cannot be used as parameters
The function needs a global declaration
answer: The default list is created once at definition time and shared by every call
questions.explain: Default arguments are evaluated once when the def runs, so every call that omits basket mutates the same list and items accumulate across calls. The fix is basket=None with basket = [] if basket is None inside the body.
questions.teach:
In Python, def is a statement that runs when execution reaches it, and what it produces is a function object. A list is mutable, meaning methods like append change that very list in place instead of making a new one. If two names point at one list, a change through either name shows up through both.

Example:
a = [1]
b = a
b.append(2)
print(a)
prints [1, 2]
hints: Read the function slowly and ask where the list called basket comes from when a caller passes only item. Think about the moment Python processes the def line itself, as opposed to the moment you call the function, and how many separate lists that could create.

Picture calling add_item('a') and then add_item('b'), without ever passing a basket. Does the second call begin with an empty list, or with whatever the first call left behind? Also notice that the function ends with return basket, so the return value is not the problem.

Three of the options make claims you can test. Lists are perfectly legal parameters. The function ends with return basket, so append returning None does not matter. And nothing here rebinds a global name, so no global statement is needed. That leaves the option about when the default list is created and how many copies exist.
questions.deep: Defaults are evaluated once and stored on the function object (see add_item.__defaults__), so the same list is reused on every call. Use None as a sentinel and build the list inside. The same trap hits dict and set, which is why dataclasses reject list defaults and want field(default_factory=list).

questions.prompt: Which three statements are true? Choose three.
options: from math import sqrt puts sqrt directly in the current namespace
A name assigned inside a function is local unless declared global
After import math as m, the name math is still usable
Indentation, not braces, defines block structure in Python
answer: from math import sqrt puts sqrt directly in the current namespace
A name assigned inside a function is local unless declared global
Indentation, not braces, defines block structure in Python
questions.explain: from X import Y binds Y itself, so you call sqrt() rather than math.sqrt(). Assignment inside a function creates a local name, which is why reassigning a module-level variable without global silently makes a second one. import math as m binds only m, so math is not defined. Blocks are defined by indentation, which makes consistent indenting part of the syntax rather than a style choice.
questions.teach:
Python tracks names in namespaces, like labelled boxes: an import or an assignment creates a name in one of them, and each function call gets its own private box. When you judge a statement about imports or scope, ask which exact name is created and in which box. Python also has no braces: where a block of code starts and ends is shown by how far a line is pushed in from the left.

Example:
import json
print(json.dumps([1]))
prints [1]
Here the name json is created, so you write json. before dumps.
hints: This is a choose-three question, so exactly one statement is false. Try to spot the false one first, and the other three are your answer. For each statement, ask which name Python actually creates, and in which namespace that name lives.

Look hard at the statement about import math as m. The word as gives the module a nickname. Ask yourself whether Python also keeps the original name next to the nickname, or whether only one name gets bound. Try to imagine typing math.pi on the very next line.

Once the odd one is set aside, the remaining three should each feel familiar: using a function with no module prefix in front of it, an assignment inside a function creating that function's own private name, and blocks being shown by spacing rather than curly braces.
questions.deep: Import statements are just name binding. from math import sqrt binds sqrt to the same object, while import math as m binds only m. Scope is decided at compile time: if a function assigns to a name anywhere, that name is local throughout it, so reading it before the assignment raises UnboundLocalError.
